title: Design a Vending Machine (OOD)
prompt: Design a vending machine. A customer selects a product, inserts money (coins/notes or card), the machine dispenses the item and returns change. Model the classes and, importantly, the machine's state machine — what the machine does when idle, when money is being inserted, when dispensing, and when a selection is sold out. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: The textbook State-pattern problem — model the machine as an explicit state machine over selection, payment, dispensing, and change.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Clarifies payment types (coins/notes/card), whether change is given, cancel/refund behavior, and inventory per slot before designing.

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Identifies VendingMachine, Product, Slot/Inventory, the State hierarchy, Payment, and CoinBank/change dispenser.

rubric.label: State machine
rubric.description: A clean explicit state machine (Idle/HasSelection/AwaitingPayment/Dispensing/OutOfService) with well-defined transitions and guarded actions per state.

rubric.label: Class design
rubric.description: State encapsulated as objects (not a mega-switch), inventory and coin-bank separated from control flow, product data immutable.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: State pattern for machine behavior, Strategy for payment methods, optional Factory for states; each justified.

rubric.label: Relationships
rubric.description: Machine composes Inventory and CoinBank; delegates behavior to current State; correct ownership.

rubric.label: API methods
rubric.description: selectProduct, insertMoney, dispense, cancel/refund; each routed through the current state.

rubric.label: SOLID principles
rubric.description: Open/closed: new states or payment methods without editing existing ones; single-responsibility across state/inventory/payment.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Insufficient funds, exact-change-only, sold out mid-transaction, cancel with refund, cannot make change, concurrent buyers.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: Card/mobile payment, promotions, multiple simultaneous selections, or a new state slot in cleanly.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Draws the state diagram clearly, walks a full purchase and a cancel path, and reasons about where guards live.

functional_requirements: Display available products with prices and stock
Accept payment (coins/notes; optionally card) and track running balance
Dispense the product when paid and in stock, and return correct change
Allow cancel with full refund of inserted money
Go out of service / restock and refill coin bank
nonfunctional_requirements: Never dispense without sufficient payment; never lose a customer's money
Deterministic behavior via an explicit state machine
Thread-safe for a single physical machine's concurrent-ish inputs
Extensible to new payment methods and states
clarifying_questions: Which payment methods — coins/notes only, or card/mobile too?
Does the machine give change, and can it be exact-change-only when low on coins?
Can a customer buy multiple items in one transaction, or one at a time?
What happens on cancel — full refund? What denominations can it return?
Do we handle restocking and an out-of-service/maintenance mode?

core_classes.name: VendingMachine
core_classes.responsibility: Context: holds current State, inventory, coin bank, and the selected product/balance; delegates every action to the current state.

core_classes.name: State (interface)
core_classes.responsibility: Encapsulates behavior for one machine state; each method either acts or is an illegal-op guard.

core_classes.name: IdleState / HasSelectionState / AwaitingPaymentState / DispensingState / OutOfServiceState
core_classes.responsibility: Concrete states implementing only the transitions legal from that state; illegal actions are no-ops or errors.

core_classes.name: Product
core_classes.responsibility: Immutable catalog item: code, name, price.

core_classes.name: Slot / Inventory
core_classes.responsibility: Tracks quantity per product code; answers availability and decrements on dispense.

core_classes.name: CoinBank / ChangeDispenser
core_classes.responsibility: Holds denomination counts; computes and dispenses change, or reports it can't make exact change.

core_classes.name: PaymentStrategy (interface)
core_classes.responsibility: Abstracts how payment is collected (cash accumulation vs card authorization).

relationships: VendingMachine (Context) has-a current State and delegates all actions to it
Concrete states implement the State interface (inheritance/polymorphism)
VendingMachine composes Inventory and CoinBank (they don't outlive the machine)
Inventory maps product codes to Product (immutable) and to quantities
VendingMachine has-a PaymentStrategy for cash vs card

design_patterns.why: Each state owns its legal transitions; replaces a brittle mega-switch and makes illegal actions impossible per state.
Add payment methods without editing the machine or states.
Reuse stateless state objects (flyweight-ish); one physical machine — but keep injectable for tests.

apis: void restock(String code, int qty) / void refillCoins(...)
state_transitions: Idle --selectProduct(valid, in stock)--> HasSelection; --select sold-out--> Idle (reject)
AwaitingPayment --balance >= price and canMakeChange--> Dispensing; --balance < price--> AwaitingPayment; --cancel--> Idle (refund)
any --stock empty everywhere / maintenance--> OutOfService --restock--> Idle
edge_cases: Insufficient funds: stay in AwaitingPayment, show remaining amount
Exact-change-only: if coin bank can't make change, refuse before dispensing and refund
Sold out at selection or between select and pay — reject and refund
Cancel mid-transaction: refund the exact inserted denominations
Overpayment: dispense and return change; if change impossible, refuse and refund
Concurrent buyers hitting one machine: serialize actions so state transitions are atomic
concurrency: A single physical machine has effectively one input stream, but model actions as atomic: synchronize state transitions so insertMoney/dispense/cancel don't interleave
Inventory deduct and coin-bank change must be atomic with the transition to Dispensing so two rapid requests can't double-dispense
If exposed as a service (many machines), each machine instance holds its own lock; no shared mutable state across machines
extensibility: New payment method (card/UPI/NFC): implement PaymentStrategy — states unchanged
New state (e.g., PromptForBag, LoyaltyScan): add a State class; existing states only reference it at their transition point
Promotions/discounts: a PricingStrategy consulted before payment
Multi-item cart: extend AwaitingPayment to accumulate a basket before dispensing
Telemetry/restock alerts: Observer on low-stock events

deep_dives.probe: Why model this as State objects instead of an enum + switch in each method? Show me what adding a new state costs in each approach.
How does the coin bank decide it can make exact change, and what do you do when it can't — greedy by denomination or something safer?
Where does the 'not enough money' guard live — in the machine, or in AwaitingPaymentState? Why does that matter for open/closed?
Between checking stock and dispensing, could the item sell out? How do you make stock-deduct + change + transition atomic?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions switch or if or enum state
followup_bank.question: That switch on state will grow with every action. How does the State pattern remove it, and what does adding a state cost then?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions payment or card or coin
followup_bank.question: How do you support cash and card without branching in the machine — a PaymentStrategy?
Walk me through making change when the coin bank is low — how do you detect exact-change-only and avoid handing out the wrong amount?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions sold out or inventory or stock
followup_bank.question: What if the item sells out between selection and payment? Where's the re-check and where does the refund happen?

tradeoffs: State objects (extensible, more classes) vs enum+switch (fewer classes, brittle) — State wins as transitions grow
Greedy change-making (simple) vs exact/dp change (correct with odd denominations) — greedy is fine for standard coins, note the limitation
Stateless shared state objects (memory-light) vs per-machine state instances (simpler)
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer treats the machine as a Context that delegates every action to an explicit State object — Idle, HasSelection, AwaitingPayment, Dispensing, OutOfService — so each state implements only its legal transitions and illegal actions are guarded per state rather than in a growing switch. Inventory and a CoinBank are composed and separated from control flow; Product is immutable; payment is a Strategy so cash and card coexist without branching. The candidate draws the state diagram, walks a full purchase plus a cancel-with-refund, and handles the sharp edges: insufficient funds, sold-out between select and pay, and exact-change-only when the coin bank can't make change (refuse before dispensing). They make stock-deduct + change + transition atomic, and show that adding a payment method or a new state is open/closed. They can justify State-vs-switch and greedy-vs-exact change tradeoffs.

interviewer_notes: The whole point of this question is the State pattern — if the candidate reaches for an enum and a switch in every method, let them, then ask what adding one state costs and steer them to State objects. Insist on a drawn state diagram with explicit transitions and on where guards live (in the state, not scattered). Push the change-making edge case: exact-change-only and can't-make-change are what separate mid from junior here. Also probe atomicity of stock-deduct + dispense. Over-engineering traps: a distributed/threaded design for a single machine, a full payment-gateway integration, or a rules engine for pricing before the core flow works. If time remains, ask for card payment (Strategy) or a multi-item cart to test extensibility.
